🤖 @saturdayrobotic Robotics World Model Reading Club #25
🎤 @ColinYu14116982 (@UofMaryland, @amazon): Contact-Rich Robot Learning from Human Videos and Tactile.
🎤 @LinfengZhaoZLF (@Stanford): Retriever: Closing the Perception-Reasoning-Action Loop for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation.
🦾 @Scav (@MissionRobotBay)

Contact-Rich Robot Learning: From Human Video → Object Flow → Tactile Residuals → Temporal Robot Agents
Bottleneck: embodiment and contact—not raw model scale—still dominate robot learning.

1️⃣ Human Video: Transfer the Object, Not the Human

Human video is our largest manipulation dataset. The transferable signal is object motion + interaction structure, not human morphology.

Object-centric flow captures embodiment-agnostic translation/rotation/trajectory.
Interaction-centric representations capture contact point, relative motion, and interaction state (approach → contact → manipulation).
GenFlowRL replaces expensive video-prediction rewards with generated object-centric δ-flow: dense flow matching + sparse stage rewards, while conditioning the policy itself.
Language-conditioned dynamics tuning + motion/semantic filtering matter; raw optical flow is too noisy.
Bounding box → keypoints → CoTracker → motion filtering enables scalable cross-embodiment datasets.
HumanEgo shows zero-shot human→robot transfer: ~92.5% average success across 4 tasks with ~30 min human video/task, without robot demos.

🔥 Hot take: the embodiment gap is not primarily visual—it is morphology + contact dynamics. Match the object and interaction, not the human body.

Video generation remains useful for imagination/planning, but compressed object flow is a better closed-loop reward/policy interface.

2️⃣ Tactile: Freeze Vision, Learn the Contact Residual

Vision gives a strong motion prior; touch supplies what vision cannot: force, shear, slip, compliance, and local geometry.

MimicTouch: human tactile demonstrations are dramatically more efficient than teleop (104 vs. 19 traj/hr for SpaceMouse; 83.3% vs. 38.5% success). Multi-modal proprioception + GelSight + audio → representation learning → imitation → real-world SAC residual RL.

OmniTacTune generalizes this idea: attach a policy-agnostic, contact-gated tactile residual to any frozen visual policy—Human-flow, Diffusion Policy, ACT, π₀.₅, etc. Dense rewards combine object flow + tactile grasp/stability + slip/safety signals.

Reported Peg-in-Hole gains: Human-flow 40→100%, Diffusion 30→90%, ACT 25→80%, π₀.₅ 15→75%, within ~40–80 min real interaction.

🔥 Hot take: don't retrain the whole robot policy to learn touch. Freeze the visual prior; learn only the residual corrections that vision cannot see.

3️⃣ ControlTac: Scale Touch Through Physical Latents

Tactile pixels are sensor-specific. The scalable abstraction should be force + contact area + pose + slip.

ControlTac generates realistic tactile images from one reference conditioned on ΔF + contact pose, enabling trajectory augmentation and improving tracking, weighing and imitation. The next step, RoboTac, extends this from static images to action-conditioned tactile dynamics.

🔥 Hot takes:

One real image + physical controls can generate useful tactile distributions.
Marker-free generation + marker recomposition enables practical augmentation.
Contact-gated residuals are more stable than letting touch fight vision everywhere.
Dense flow + grasp + slip rewards beat sparse success signals for contact-rich RL.
Sensor-specific pixels are a historical accident; shared physical features are the scalable latent.
Better perception/data alone cannot close the final hardware/compliance gap. Humans dynamically change stiffness; rigid robots cannot.

🎯 Long-term goal: a tactile world model that imagines contact under candidate actions and schedules compliance before contact—not merely reacts after impact.

4️⃣ Retriever: Robotics Needs a “PyTorch” for Closed-Loop Agents

Long-horizon robotics has another missing layer: the harness connecting System 2 reasoning/VLMs, System 1 skill VLAs, memory and high-rate control.

Retriever proposes Flow + Clock + Sync + Runtime:
Temporal compositionality
Asynchronous multi-rate execution
First-class closed loops
Explicit synchronization
Deterministic replay
Hardware/backend abstraction

30 Hz perception → 2 Hz skill VLA → 200 Hz controller can run concurrently without reasoning blocking control. Belief, replanning and skill-progress triggers close the loop.

🔥 Hot take: robotics doesn't just need another foundation model. It needs a programming model with explicit temporal semantics—one where agents can be composed, debugged, replayed, ported and eventually trained at scale.

The Bigger Bet

The trajectory is surprisingly coherent:
Human video learns WHAT should happen → object/interaction flow bridges embodiments → tactile residuals learn HOW contact feels → tactile world models anticipate contact → temporal runtimes turn these modules into scalable closed-loop agents.

The next frontier may therefore be less about bigger policies and more about better abstractions: object motion, interaction state, physical contact variables, and time itself.

Sporting bodies worldwide have been rewriting the rules for trans and gender diverse athletes, most recently the IOC's March 2026 policy requiring SRY gene screening. Our new review in the International Journal of Sports Medicine asks a simple question: What evidence are these policies built on?

The short answer is not much.

We traced the history of eligibility rules from 2003 to now, mapped current policies across 16 sports, and assessed them against the science. What we found:

🔬 Gender-affirming hormone therapy does produce real physiological changes. Within three months of starting estradiol, haemoglobin and haematocrit fall into female reference ranges.

📊 The most comprehensive evidence to date, a meta-analysis of 52 studies and 6,485 people, found that trans women on hormone therapy have comparable upper body strength, lower body strength, and VO2max to cisgender women. Certainty of that evidence is graded low to very low, which is exactly why more research is needed.

🧬 SRY is a gene that switches on briefly during embryonic development to initiate testis formation. It has no known function in adult tissue and does not determine adult muscle mass, strength, or athletic performance. Using it as a universal eligibility test is not supported by biology.

🏅 Despite more than 20 years of eligibility at Olympic and elite level, trans women have neither medalled nor dominated any women's sport.

We argue that fairness and safety cannot be settled by biology alone, and propose a framework where inclusion is the default, restrictions are proportionate to the actual demands of each sport, and policies are reviewed as evidence improves.

Trans and gender diverse people already participate in sport and physical activity at lower rates, with real consequences for physical and mental health.

Lastly, these policies do not only affect trans athletes. Highly policed eligibility rules increase scrutiny of all women's bodies, particularly women who do not fit narrow expectations of femininity.

Open access and free to read: https://t.co/jPYNeoewXi

Led by Ananya Krishna and Séverine Lamon at Deakin University, with Carlie Bauer, Kimberley Way, Bernadette Jones-Freeman and our own Prof Ada Cheung.

One AI training task tells a company almost nothing about you

It takes hundreds before they can trust you at all
A single voice clip, gameplay session, or preference ranking can't prove you're consistent, careful, or reliable

Only a pattern across many contributions can show that

The problem is most platforms only track that pattern inside one task category

Switch to a different type of work and your history resets to zero, even though you're the same contributor

@KGeN_IO takes a different approach
> It treats reputation as one continuous profile instead of something that resets per task. Gameplay, voice data, social activity,
all of it feeds into the same identity instead of living in separate silos

The scoring itself breaks into five parts:
proof you're human, proof of consistency, proof of skill, proof of economic participation, and proof of network. Each one measures something different, but they combine into a single score that travels with you across every task type you touch,

That reputation layer isn't just theoretical
It's the same infrastructure Humyn Labs is building on for its Proof of Expert system, which sources verified human data to train AI models

So the more you contribute on KGeN, the stronger your standing gets everywhere that reputation is used, not just in the specific task where you earned it.

That's a meaningfully different definition of "putting in the work" than most Web3 platforms operate on. Most systems treat every task as its own isolated transaction: you show up, you deliver, you get paid, and your history doesn't follow you anywhere else

KGeN is betting that reputation should compound instead of reset, the same way trust works between actual people

Whether that bet pays off depends on adoption outside KGeN's own ecosystem
A portable reputation score is only as valuable as the number of platforms willing to read and respect it, Right now that list includes @Teamhumynlabs , but the real test is whether more AI labs and Web3 platforms start treating this as a standard rather than a nice to have

Should reputation always carry over like this, or does it make more sense for platforms to reset per task type?

Think about how humans learn a new skill.

You don’t become good at something by reading about it once.

You practice.
You make mistakes.
You try again.
You repeat the same task in different ways until your brain starts to understand what to do.

Robots need that same kind of experience.

The problem is, teaching a robot how to perform real world tasks requires A LOT of training data  and collecting that data in labs is slow, expensive and difficult to scale.

This is where @axisrobotics comes in.

Instead of keeping robot training inside expensive labs, Axis lets ordinary people contribute to the process.

And you contribute to the process by:

→ Open a website and control a virtual robot with your keyboard or mouse

→ Perform simple tasks like picking up and arranging objects

→ And your actions become training data that can help real robots learn.

They’re also using phones to capture real human movements and building tools that can automatically generate thousands of different scenarios for robots to practice.

And honestly, this is the part I find interesting.

Axis is basically turning human experience into robot experience.

Every small movement we make like picking something up, moving it, arranging it, reaching for something can become another example a robot learns from.

It’s almost like giving robots the opportunity to learn from millions of people instead of relying on a handful of robotics labs.

That’s the bigger idea behind Axis.

Robot intelligence shouldn’t be built by a few people in a lab.

It can be built from the everyday actions and experiences of people everywhere.

And Axis is building the data engine to make that possible.
